etymology: Hebrew Machlah, perhaps “disease” or “weakness,” the eldest of the five daughters of Zelophehad of the tribe of Manasseh.
biblical_def: Mahlah was the eldest of the five daughters of Zelophehad, the son of Hepher, of the family of Manasseh the son of Joseph (Num 26:33). Her father died in the wilderness for his own sin, having no sons, and so his name stood in danger of being blotted out from among his family for want of an heir. Mahlah and her four sisters — Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah — came and stood before Moses, Eleazar the priest, the princes, and all the congregation at the door of the tabernacle, and asked that they might have a possession among the brethren of their father, that his name be not done away (Num 27:1–4). Their petition was no demand of self-will, but a request made in faith and in order, that the inheritance of their house in the LORD’s land might be preserved. Moses brought their cause before the LORD, and the LORD judged that they spake right, and gave them an inheritance among their father’s brethren (Num 27:5–7). Afterward, that no tribe lose its allotted portion, they were charged to marry within the family of the tribe of their father (Num 36:6, 11). So Mahlah received her inheritance in the day Joshua divided the land (Jos 17:3). She stands as a witness that the daughters of faith honour the covenant order even as they seek their portion in the inheritance of the LORD.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; she witnesses that the daughters of faith seek their inheritance within the covenant order God appoints.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the petition of Zelophehad’s daughters was not a demand for autonomy but a request made in faith and in order, granted by God within the law of inheritance and bounded by the requirement to marry within their tribe (Num 36). The modern reader is tempted to read Mahlah as a heroine of self-assertion against an oppressive order; the text gives no such thing. She and her sisters came humbly before Moses and the congregation, sought the preservation of their father’s name in the LORD’s land, and received their portion by the LORD’s own judgment — then submitted to the very ordering that kept each tribe’s inheritance whole.

Mahlah’s cause teaches that God’s law is no enemy to the lawful claims of His daughters but their surest refuge. Where men might have let the inheritance lapse, the LORD Himself secured it; where men might have feared the loss to the tribes, the LORD ordered the marriages so that no portion strayed. Inheritance, covenant, tribe, faith, and order — these are the biblical categories in which Mahlah’s story is rightly read, and in them she shines as a daughter who honoured both her father’s name and her God’s appointed way.

etymology: Hebrew Choglah, perhaps “partridge,” one of the five daughters of Zelophehad of the tribe of Manasseh.
biblical_def: Hoglah was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad the son of Hepher, of the family of Manasseh the son of Joseph (Num 26:33). With her sisters Mahlah, Noah, Milcah, and Tirzah she stood before Moses, Eleazar the priest, and the whole congregation to ask that an inheritance be given them among their father’s brethren, since he had died in the wilderness without sons (Num 27:1–4). The LORD judged their cause to be just, and through this case He gave Israel a statute of judgment: if a man die and have no son, his inheritance should pass to his daughter (Num 27:8). Thus Hoglah and her sisters were the occasion of a lasting ordinance in the law of inheritance, by which the LORD provided that no faithful house should lose its portion in the land for want of a male heir. Yet the same law that granted them their inheritance also ordered that they marry within the family of their father’s tribe, that the inheritance of the children of Israel remove not from tribe to tribe (Num 36:6–9). Hoglah obeyed, and was married within the families of Manasseh (Num 36:11). She is a quiet witness that the LORD honours faith and preserves inheritance, and that His daughters receive their portion within the bounds of His covenant order, not apart from it.

etymology: Hebrew Milcah, “queen” or “counsel,” one of the five daughters of Zelophehad of the tribe of Manasseh.
biblical_def: Milcah was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad the son of Hepher, of the family of Manasseh the son of Joseph (Num 26:33). She must be distinguished from the earlier Milcah, the daughter of Haran and wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, who bore him eight sons and was grandmother of Rebekah (Gen 11:29; 22:20–23); the two are different women, and only the name is shared. This Milcah of Manasseh, with her sisters Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, and Tirzah, came before Moses and the congregation when their father died without sons in the wilderness, and sought a possession among their father’s brethren that his name be not done away (Num 27:1–4). The LORD declared their cause just, and gave them an inheritance (Num 27:7). When the heads of the fathers of the tribe of Gilead feared that the daughters’ marriage outside the tribe might carry their portion away, the LORD ordered that they marry within the family of their father, that no inheritance pass from tribe to tribe (Num 36:1–9). Milcah obeyed and married within the families of Manasseh (Num 36:11). She stands among the daughters who, by faith and in submission to the LORD’s appointed order, both received their inheritance in the land and kept it within the covenant bounds He set.

The principle to recover is that the petition of Zelophehad’s daughters was not a demand for autonomy but a request made in faith and in order, granted by God within the law of inheritance and bounded by the requirement to marry within their tribe (Num 36). Milcah of Manasseh is sometimes pressed into a modern tale of women claiming rights against an order; the text shows instead a daughter who sought the preservation of her father’s name, received her portion by the LORD’s judgment, and married within her tribe as His law required.

etymology: Hebrew Tirtsah, “pleasantness” or “delight,” the youngest of the five daughters of Zelophehad of the tribe of Manasseh.
biblical_def: Tirzah was the youngest of the five daughters of Zelophehad the son of Hepher, of the family of Manasseh the son of Joseph (Num 26:33). She is to be distinguished from the city Tirzah, a royal seat of the northern kingdom and a place praised for its beauty (Song 6:4; 1Ki 14:17); the daughter and the city bear the same pleasant name but are not the same. With her sisters Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, and Milcah, Tirzah stood before Moses, Eleazar, and all the congregation when their father died without sons, and asked for a possession among their father’s brethren that his name be not done away (Num 27:1–4). The LORD declared their cause just and gave them an inheritance, and through them established the statute that a sonless man’s inheritance pass to his daughters (Num 27:7–8). When the tribe’s elders feared the inheritance might pass away by marriage, the LORD commanded that the daughters marry within their father’s tribe, so that the inheritance of Israel not be removed from tribe to tribe (Num 36:6–9). Tirzah obeyed and was married within the families of Manasseh (Num 36:11), and received her portion in the day Joshua divided the land (Jos 17:3). The youngest of the five, her name meaning delight, she stands with her sisters as a witness that the LORD’s daughters find their inheritance and their delight within the order of His covenant.

etymology: Hebrew Tola, “worm” or “scarlet,” a judge of Israel of the tribe of Issachar who arose after Abimelech.
biblical_def: Tola the son of Puah, the son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, arose to defend Israel after the bloody usurpation of Abimelech, and he judged Israel twenty and three years (Jud 10:1–2). He must be distinguished from the earlier Tola, the firstborn son of Issachar himself (Gen 46:13), whose name he bore. This judge dwelt in Shamir in mount Ephraim, and when he had judged Israel for his appointed years, he died and was buried in Shamir. Of his deeds the Scripture records almost nothing; he is one of the so-called minor judges, of whom we learn little beyond their tribe, their years, and their burial. Yet the brevity of the account is itself a testimony, for Tola arose “to defend Israel” in the wake of Abimelech’s self-exalting reign, when the land was torn by a man who had slain his seventy brethren to make himself king. After such violence the LORD raised up a quiet deliverer, and Israel had rest under his hand for more than a score of years. Tola stands as a witness to the unsung mercies of God in the days of the judges, and to the worth of the faithful servant whose chief record is that he defended God’s people and gave the land peace, though no great battle bears his name.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the worth of the faithful servant whose labours are little recorded. Of Tola the Scripture says only that he arose to defend Israel, judged twenty and three years, and was buried in Shamir; yet in that brevity lies a great mercy, for he was raised up after Abimelech’s murderous reign to give the land rest. The LORD honours quiet faithfulness, and not every deliverer must have a great battle bearing his name.

Tola’s nearly silent record rebukes the modern hunger for spectacle and self-display. The judge who simply defends God’s people and keeps the peace, then lies down in his fathers’ field, is no lesser servant than the one whose exploits fill a chapter. The dictionary marks how Scripture esteems the hidden, steadfast labour by which God’s people are kept — a worth measured not by fame but by faithfulness before the LORD.

etymology: Hebrew Kimham, perhaps “longing” or “pining,” a son of Barzillai the Gileadite whom David took over Jordan and provided for.
biblical_def: Chimham was, it is thought, a son of Barzillai the Gileadite, the aged and wealthy man who had sustained David with provision at Mahanaim during Absalom’s rebellion. When David returned over Jordan in triumph, he would have brought Barzillai to Jerusalem to feast him at the king’s own table; but Barzillai, being fourscore years old, declined, asking only to die in his own city by the grave of his father and mother. He commended Chimham to the king in his stead, saying, “Behold thy servant Chimham; let him go over with my lord the king; and do to him what shall seem good unto thee” (2Sa 19:37). So David took Chimham over Jordan and showed him the kindness that the old man would not take for himself, fulfilling his promise to honour the house of Barzillai (1Ki 2:7). From this there remained a place near Bethlehem called “the habitation of Chimham,” or the lodging-place of Chimham, where travellers later stayed (Jer 41:17). Some have thought the place was granted out of David’s own patrimony in Bethlehem to Barzillai’s son. Chimham stands as a witness to the king’s faithfulness in repaying a kindness shown in the day of trouble, and to the honour that descends upon a house through the loyalty of its father; the good done to David in his distress was remembered and returned to Barzillai’s son for generations.
webster_summary: A son of Barzillai the Gileadite whom David took over Jordan to honour, leaving a place called the habitation of Chimham.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the faithfulness that repays kindness shown in the day of distress. Barzillai sustained David when he fled from Absalom; David, returning in triumph, would not forget it, and took Barzillai’s son Chimham over Jordan to honour him, charging even Solomon to keep that kindness toward the house. Gratitude that endures and repays is a mark of the upright, and the king of Israel is here a faint shadow of the King who forgets none of His servants’ labours of love.

Chimham’s lasting habitation by Bethlehem also commends the honour that descends upon a house through the loyalty of its father. Barzillai’s faithfulness in a dark hour purchased a blessing for his son and a name that endured by the city of David. So the LORD often visits the children of the faithful with mercy for their fathers’ sake, and the good done in one generation bears fruit in the next.

etymology: Hebrew Ira, perhaps “watchful” or “city,” a Jairite who was a chief ruler about David.
biblical_def: Ira the Jairite is named once in the Scripture, at the close of the list of David’s chief officers: “And Ira also the Jairite was a chief ruler about David” (2Sa 20:26). He is called a Jairite, likely of the family of Jair of the tribe of Manasseh, whose villages lay in Gilead. The phrase rendered “chief ruler” is, in the Hebrew, the word commonly used for a priest, and so some have understood him to hold a place of priestly or chief counsel near the king’s person, a confidential officer of the court. He is to be distinguished from Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite and Ira the Ithrite, two of David’s mighty men (2Sa 23:26, 38); the name was not uncommon. Of Ira the Jairite nothing more is told than this single notice, that he stood among the great men about David, trusted and honoured in the king’s service. Yet even so brief a mention preserves his name forever in the inspired record. Ira the Jairite stands as a witness that the LORD takes account of the unnamed labours of faithful men, and that to serve near the throne of God’s anointed, in whatever quiet office, is no small dignity, though Scripture record of it but a line.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of the faithful servant whose labour fills but a single line of Scripture. Ira the Jairite is named once, a chief ruler about David, and no deed of his is recorded; yet his name is kept forever in the inspired record. The LORD takes account of the unnamed and the little-noticed, and to serve near the throne of His anointed, in whatever quiet office, is no small honour.

Ira’s single mention also teaches the reader the discipline of distinguishing the men of Scripture who share a name. Three men called Ira stand among David’s great ones, and the careful reader keeps them apart. The brevity that might tempt us to pass him by is itself a mercy, reminding us that God’s book has room even for the servant of one line, and that faithfulness, not fame, is the measure He keeps.

etymology: Hebrew Avishag, perhaps “my father is a wanderer” or “cause of wandering,” the Shunammite who cherished David in his old age.
biblical_def: Abishag was a young woman of Shunem, very fair, sought out by the servants of David when the king was old and stricken in years and gat no heat though they covered him with clothes (1Ki 1:1–3). She was brought to cherish the king and to lie in his bosom that he might have warmth; and she ministered to him, but the king knew her not (1Ki 1:4). So she became, by this service, of the king’s household, though not his wife in the full sense. After David’s death, Adonijah, who had once exalted himself to be king, came to Bathsheba and asked that Abishag the Shunammite be given him to wife (1Ki 2:13–17). To take the woman of the late king was, in the custom of that age, a grasping after the throne itself; and Solomon discerned in the request a renewed bid for the kingdom. He answered, “Ask for him the kingdom also,” and that same day sent Benaiah to put Adonijah to death (1Ki 2:22–25). Thus Abishag, an innocent and faithful servant, became the occasion that unmasked Adonijah’s ambition and sealed his doom. She stands as a witness to the providence of God, who used a quiet handmaid to expose a proud usurper, and to establish Solomon’s throne in peace according to the word the LORD had spoken.
webster_summary: The Shunammite who cherished the aged David; Adonijah’s request for her unmasked his ambition and cost him his life.
webster_full: ABISHAG, a fair young woman of Shunem (1Ki 1:3).
She was brought to cherish David in his old age.
She ministered to the king, but he knew her not (1Ki 1:4).
Adonijah asked to have her to wife after David’s death (1Ki 2:17).
Solomon discerned a bid for the throne and slew Adonijah (1Ki 2:22–25).
scriptures: So they sought for a fair damsel throughout all the coasts of Israel, and found Abishag a Shunammite, and brought her to the king.
And the damsel was very fair, and cherished the king, and ministered to him: but the king knew her not.
And he said, Speak, I pray thee, unto Solomon the king, (for he will not say thee nay,) that he give me Abishag the Shunammite to wife.

And king Solomon answered and said unto his mother, And why dost thou ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? ask for him the kingdom also; for he is mine elder brother; even for him, and for Abiathar the priest, and for Joab the son of Zeruiah.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; she witnesses the providence of God, who used a quiet handmaid to unmask a proud usurper.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence of God working through the lowly and the innocent. Abishag was a faithful young servant who cherished the dying king; yet through her, when Adonijah grasped at her to grasp at the throne, the LORD unmasked the usurper’s ambition and established Solomon’s kingdom in peace. God orders even the quiet ministries of His humble servants to the working out of His purposes for His anointed.

Abishag’s account also teaches that ambition cloaks itself in soft requests. Adonijah did not openly seize the crown; he asked only for a woman of the late king’s house. But Solomon discerned the heart beneath the request, for to claim the king’s woman was to claim the kingdom. The wise must look past the gentle wording of proud men to the thing they truly seek; and the LORD, who searches the heart, brought the hidden ambition into the light and judged it.
roots_summary: The name perhaps means “my father is a wanderer,” borne by the Shunammite who cherished David.

usage: Like Abishag, the lowly and innocent servant may be the instrument of God’s providence.
Abishag’s account teaches that proud ambition often cloaks itself in soft and gentle requests.
Through her quiet ministry the LORD unmasked a usurper and established Solomon’s throne in peace.

etymology: Hebrew Sheba, “oath” or “seven,” a Benjamite, a man of Belial, who led a revolt against David.
biblical_def: Sheba the son of Bichri was a Benjamite, called “a man of Belial,” who raised the standard of revolt against David in the bitter days after Absalom’s fall, when the men of Israel and the men of Judah strove over the king (2Sa 20:1). He blew a trumpet and cried, “We have no part in David, neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse: every man to his tents, O Israel” (2Sa 20:1). At this word every man of Israel went up from after David to follow Sheba, though the men of Judah clave unto their king (2Sa 20:2). David, judging this rebellion more dangerous than Absalom’s had been, sent Joab and the host in pursuit. Sheba fled through all the tribes to Abel of Beth-maachah, a fortified city in the far north, and there Joab besieged him and cast up a mount against the wall (2Sa 20:14–15). But a wise woman of the city treated with Joab, and the men of Abel cut off the head of Sheba and threw it over the wall to him, that the city be not destroyed; and Joab withdrew (2Sa 20:21–22). Thus the revolt collapsed with the death of its author. Sheba stands as a warning of the man who sows division among God’s people, despising the LORD’s anointed; his rebellion, raised in a moment by a blast of the trumpet, ended swiftly in his own destruction.
webster_summary: A Benjamite and man of Belial who raised revolt against David, crying “We have no part in David,” and perished at Abel.
webster_full: SHEBA THE SON OF BICHRI, a Benjamite, a man of Belial (2Sa 20:1).
He blew a trumpet and led Israel in revolt against David.
He cried, “We have no part in David” (2Sa 20:1).
He fled to Abel of Beth-maachah, where Joab besieged him (2Sa 20:14–15).
The men of Abel cut off his head and ended the revolt (2Sa 20:22).
scriptures: And there happened to be there a man of Belial, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjamite: and he blew a trumpet, and said, We have no part in David, neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse: every man to his tents, O Israel.
So every man of Israel went up from after David, and followed Sheba the son of Bichri: but the men of Judah clave unto their king, from Jordan even to Jerusalem.

The matter is not so: but a man of mount Ephraim, Sheba the son of Bichri by name, hath lifted up his hand against the king, even against David: deliver him only, and I will depart from the city. And the woman said unto Joab, Behold, his head shall be thrown to thee over the wall.

Then the woman went unto all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri, and cast it out to Joab. And he blew a trumpet, and they retired from the city, every man to his tent. And Joab returned to Jerusalem unto the king.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; he stands as a warning against the man who sows division and despises the LORD’s anointed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the wickedness of sowing division among God’s people against His anointed. Sheba, a man of Belial, blew his trumpet and cried, “We have no part in David,” and drew Israel after him into rebellion. To despise the LORD’s chosen king and to rend the people from their head was a great sin; and the revolt, raised in a moment by a self-willed man, ended swiftly in his own destruction.

Sheba’s rising teaches how easily a multitude is led astray by a discontented man with a trumpet and a slogan. Every man of Israel went up after him at a word, though the men of Judah clave to their king. The dictionary marks the abiding danger of the demagogue who exploits a season of strife to set himself up by tearing others down; his end is the warning. “We have no part in David” was the cry of rebellion against the type of Christ; to have no part in great David’s greater Son is the ruin of the soul.
roots_summary: The name means “oath” or “seven,” borne by the Benjamite who led revolt against David.

usage: Like Sheba, the man who sows division against God’s anointed sins greatly and comes to ruin.

etymology: From Hebrew Abel, the city Abel of Beth-maachah, where a wise woman treated with Joab and delivered the city.
biblical_def: The wise woman of Abel of Beth-maachah is unnamed in Scripture, yet honoured for her wisdom in delivering her city from destruction. When Sheba the son of Bichri, fleeing his failed revolt against David, had taken refuge in Abel, Joab and his host besieged the city and cast up a mount against the wall, battering to throw it down (2Sa 20:14–15). Then a wise woman cried from the city, asking to speak with Joab, and reasoned with him: “I am one of them that are peaceable and faithful in Israel: thou seekest to destroy a city and a mother in Israel: why wilt thou swallow up the inheritance of the LORD?” (2Sa 20:19). Joab answered that he sought not to destroy, but only the rebel Sheba; deliver him, and he would depart. The woman replied that Sheba’s head should be thrown over the wall; and she went to all the people in her wisdom, and they cut off the head of Sheba and cast it out to Joab, who blew the trumpet of retreat and withdrew (2Sa 20:21–22). By her counsel a whole city was spared, and a rebel’s revolt undone. She stands as a witness that the LORD has set His wisdom even in the unnamed and the lowly, and that one faithful soul, pleading for the inheritance of the LORD and for peace, may turn away wrath and save a multitude alive.
webster_summary: An unnamed wise woman of Abel of Beth-maachah who treated with Joab and saved her city by delivering up Sheba’s head.
webster_full: THE WISE WOMAN OF ABEL, an unnamed woman of Abel of Beth-maachah (2Sa 20:16).

By her counsel the people cut off Sheba’s head (2Sa 20:22).
She thus saved the whole city from destruction.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; she witnesses that the LORD sets His wisdom in the lowly to turn away wrath and save a multitude.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD has set His wisdom even in the unnamed and the lowly, and that one faithful soul may turn away wrath and save a multitude. The wise woman of Abel did not lead an army nor hold an office; she reasoned with Joab from the wall, pleaded for the inheritance of the LORD, and by her counsel persuaded a whole city to deliver up the rebel and live. Wisdom and faithfulness, not station, made her a deliverer.

Her plea, “Why wilt thou swallow up the inheritance of the LORD?”, teaches a love for the peace and preservation of God’s people that puts away the one troubler for the good of the many. She did not shield the rebel Sheba; she gave him up, that the city of God’s inheritance might stand. So the dictionary marks her as a figure of the peaceable and faithful in Israel, whose wisdom prizes the good of the whole covenant people above the cause of the one who has lifted his hand against the king.
